name: Psoralen (PUVA, bergamot oil tanning)

lead: Psoralens are light-sensitizing compounds found in plants such as figs, celery and citrus, including bergamot oil. With UVA light they darken skin, which is why tanning activators once used them to get a deeper tan faster. Doctors use them in PUVA therapy for conditions like psoriasis and vitiligo.

The chain is photochemical: psoralen enters the skin and, when hit by UVA, binds DNA and triggers damage responses and pigment production. Psoralen-based tanning activators were used in sun products until 1996, when they were banned after being found photocarcinogenic. Its cosmetic tanning effect is documented mainly from that older use.

paras: Historically, psoralen or bergamot oil was applied in tanning products before sun or UVA exposure. In medicine, PUVA is delivered under clinical supervision for skin conditions. Bergamot-oil use for tanning today is a fringe practice.

Documented harms include severe phototoxic burns and skin loss after sunbathing with psoralen products. Long-term PUVA is associated with higher skin cancer rates, including squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma, and psoralens are described as photocarcinogenic.

angle.text: Psoralen and bergamot oil were used in tanning products because they make skin respond more strongly to UVA, so users could darken faster. It is used medically as PUVA for skin conditions. Its tanning use was restricted in 1996 after phototoxic and photocarcinogenic findings.

lead: Psoralen is the parent compound of the linear furanocoumarins, plant-derived photosensitizing chemicals that bind DNA when exposed to UVA light. They occur in figs, celery, parsley, citrus fruit and, in the form of bergapten and bergamottin, in bergamot oil [1].

Medically, psoralen plus UVA (PUVA) is used to treat psoriasis, vitiligo and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma [1][2]. In tanning culture, psoralen-containing products, including bergamot oil, have been used as tanning activators that increase pigmentation after sun exposure. Psoralen-based tanning activators were used in sun products until 1996, when they were banned after being found photocarcinogenic [1][3].

Psoralens are phototoxic: some people suffered severe skin loss after sunbathing with products containing them [1]. Long-term PUVA treatment is associated with higher skin cancer rates, including squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma [1][2][4].
infobox: Fig, celery, parsley, citrus, bergamot oil [1]

paras: With UVA light, psoralen forms monoadducts and interstrand cross-links with thymine bases in DNA, which can induce apoptosis [1]. This photochemistry is also exploited in molecular biology to study DNA and RNA structure [5]. In skin, the damage response stimulates melanocytes, which is why psoralen plus light darkens skin.

PUVA treats vitiligo, psoriasis, eczema, graft-versus-host disease, mycosis fungoides and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with psoralen given orally, topically or in baths before UVA exposure [2]. Ancient Egyptian use of Ammi majus juice plus sunlight on vitiligo is described, and modern PUVA began in 1940s Cairo with methoxsalen [2]. Narrowband UVB is now more commonly used for vitiligo [2].

Bergamot oil contains psoralens and was used in cosmetic tanning preparations. Psoralen-containing tanning activators were sold in sunscreens until 1996, and in 1980 and 1981 studies linked 5-methoxypsoralen, a tanning additive, to lethal and mutagenic effects and tumours in mice [1]. Health authorities banned the activators in July 1996 [3].

No studies were found of psoralen or bergamot oil as a cosmetic tanning aid. Studies of medical PUVA exist: the PUVA Follow-Up Study reported an elevated risk of malignant melanoma in psoriasis patients treated with methoxsalen and UVA [4]. Registered trials compare PUVA with other light therapies or drugs for vitiligo and hand and foot dermatoses [6][7].

Short-term effects include nausea, vomiting, redness, itching, dry skin and pain from phototoxic nerve damage [1]. Long-term oral PUVA is associated with higher skin cancer rates, notably squamous cell carcinoma [2]. Psoralens are described as photocarcinogenic [1].
